target.title: Hearing Lips: Improving Lip Reading by Distilling Speech Recognizers
target.venue: The Thirty-Fourth AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-20)
target.version: AAAI-20 proceedings version (doi-10.1609-aaai.v34i04.6174); arXiv:1911.11502 v1 (2019-11-26) is the first public version, same tables and numbers

read.pdf: Figures 1–3; Tables 1–5; all sections and the complete reference list read

entries.text: LIBS distills multi-granularity speech-recognizer knowledge to train a lip reader.
entries.condition: A pre-trained speech recognizer supplies audio-side features and predictions during lip-reader training.
entries.quote:
This is achieved, speciﬁcally, by distilling multi-
granularity knowledge from speech recognizers to lip readers.

entries.text: Authors claim, to their knowledge, this is the first attempt to transfer knowledge along this speech-recognition-to-lip-reading line.
entries.condition: Novelty claim in the introduction; not an independently established priority claim.
entries.quote: This is to our best knowledge the ﬁrst attempt along this line

entries.text: The paper distinguishes its feature-level recurrent-network distillation from earlier CNN-focused feature-level KD.
entries.condition: Authors describe feature-level knowledge transfer between recurrent speech-recognition and lip-reading networks.

entries.text: Distillation losses operate at sequence, context, and frame levels, alongside the lip-reader base loss.
entries.condition: Total objective is base lip-reading loss plus three weighted KD losses.
entries.quote: Knowledge is distilled at sequence-, context-, and frame-level to enable the features of multi-granularity to be transferred from teacher network to student.

entries.text: Context-level KD uses an LCS filter to retain ordered character matches between ASR hypotheses and ground-truth transcripts; Chinese matches are defined by shared Pinyin.
entries.condition: Used during training to select context vectors; it is not described as user correction at inference.

entries.text: Frame-level alignment is learned by audio-encoder states attending over video-encoder states, then aligned features are distilled.
entries.condition: Soft attention provides audio-to-video correspondence for mismatched temporal lengths and synchronization.

entries.text: Authors identify asynchronous audio/video sequences and imperfect speech-recognition predictions as the two main distillation challenges.
entries.condition: Different sampling rates and imperfect ASR outputs motivate alignment and filtering.

entries.text: In preliminary experiments, video attending to audio performed worse, so the authors retain only audio attending to video for frame-level KD.
entries.condition: Directionality choice for frame-level alignment; no quantitative ablation is reported here.

entries.text: CMLR is reported to contain over 100,000 natural Mandarin sentences, over 3,000 Chinese characters, and 20,000 phrases.
entries.condition: CMLR dataset, collected from China Network Television; reported dataset totals, not test-set counts.

entries.text: LRS2 contains more than 45,000 BBC spoken sentences; its provided development and test partition is based on broadcast date.
entries.condition: LRS2 benchmark; train/validation development set and test set separated according to broadcast date.

entries.text: The experiments follow the supplied dataset partitions.
entries.condition: CMLR follows its provided partition; LRS2 uses its broadcast-date partition.

entries.text: CER and WER use substitutions plus deletions plus insertions divided by reference character/word count; LRS2 reports CER, WER, unigram BLEU, while CMLR reports CER and BLEU only.
entries.condition: CMLR word boundaries are unavailable because Chinese sentences are continuous character strings.

entries.text: Training uses length-based curriculum learning, starting with short sentences and increasing sequence length, plus scheduled sampling.
entries.condition: CMLR and LRS2 training sets lack word-boundary annotations; sentences are grouped by length.

entries.text: Scheduled-sampling rates are 0.7–1 for CMLR and 0–0.25 for LRS2; decoding beam widths are 1 and 4 respectively.
entries.condition: CMLR and LRS2 experiments; paper says beam search is used for fair comparison.

entries.text: LRS2 adds visual-feature pre-training on word excerpts using a CNN pre-trained on MV-LRS; frozen features are used, with the word length increased to at most 16 before end-to-end training.
entries.condition: LRS2 only; pre-training on its pre-train set, followed by end-to-end training on the training set.

entries.text: CMLR video frames are 64×128 grayscale images; VGG-M consumes five lip frames per step with a two-frame step advance.
entries.unit: pixels; frames per input; frame step
entries.condition: CMLR visual input preprocessing and feature extraction.

entries.text: CMLR uses a two-layer bidirectional GRU encoder (cell size 256), two-layer unidirectional GRU decoder (cell size 512), and a 1,779-token character vocabulary retaining characters occurring more than 20 times plus special tokens.
entries.unit: layers; cell size; layers; cell size; frequency threshold; vocabulary items
entries.condition: CMLR lip-reader architecture and character vocabulary.

entries.text: CMLR initial learning rate is 0.0003; it is halved after four epochs without training-error improvement, and warm-up is used.
entries.condition: CMLR lip-reader training; warm-up is cited as a measure to prevent over-fitting.

entries.text: LRS2 uses 112×112 mouth-region images and a CNN with a five-frame 3D-convolution filter; its lip reader has three-layer bidirectional LSTM encoder and three-layer unidirectional LSTM decoder, cell sizes 256 and 512, and 29 output tokens.
entries.unit: pixels; frames; layers; cell size; layers; cell size; output tokens
entries.condition: LRS2 visual input and lip-reader architecture; vocabulary consists of 26 letters and [sos], [eos], [pad].

entries.text: LRS2 learning rates are 0.0008 for pre-training and 0.0001 for training, halved after three epochs without training-error improvement.
entries.condition: LRS2 lip-reader training.

entries.text: KD balance weights (λ1, λ2, λ3) are (10, 40, 10) on CMLR and (2, 10, 10) on LRS2; the authors selected them by grid search.
entries.condition: Weights apply to sequence-, context-, and frame-level KD losses respectively.

entries.text: Speech recognizers are trained using CMLR/LRS2 audio plus AISHELL for CMLR and LibriSpeech for LRS2.
entries.condition: Audio teacher training data; exact partitions used are not specified (see t77).

entries.text: Speech inputs use 240-dimensional fbank features sampled at 16 kHz with 25 ms windows and 10 ms steps.
entries.unit: feature dimensions; Hz; ms window; ms step
entries.condition: Audio features for the speech-recognizer teacher.

entries.text: CMLR tests three speech-recognizer teachers: Teacher 1 matches the student GRU dimensions; Teacher 2 uses cell size 512; Teacher 3 uses a three-layer pyramidal bidirectional GRU encoder.
entries.unit: teacher variants; Teacher 1 cell size; Teacher 2 cell size; Teacher 3 encoder layers
entries.condition: CMLR teacher-model generalization experiment; Teacher 1 uses 2-layer bi-GRU encoder and 2-layer uni-GRU decoder.
entries.quote: For CMLR dataset, speciﬁcally, three different speech recognizer architectures are considered to verify the generalization of LIBS.

entries.text: Teacher 2 has a better ASR score than Teacher 1 but produces a worse lip-reading student; the authors attribute this to mismatched feature dimensions.
entries.condition: CMLR teacher comparison; direct distillation in the same feature dimension is said to work better.
entries.quote:
This is because the feature di-
mensions of Teacher 2 speech recognizer and lip reader are different.

entries.quote: the performance discrepancy is as large as 10.4% vs. 39.5% in terms of character error rate for speech recognition and lip reading, respectively (Chung et al. 2017).

questions.q: Do the tables support the broad claim that LIBS is state of the art on both CMLR and LRS2?
questions.answer: CMLR Table 5 shows LIBS ahead of WAS and CSSMCM on CER. LRS2 Table 5 instead reports lower CER for CTC/Attention than LIBS and lower WER for CTC/Attention and TM-seq2seq; the paper itself notes TM-seq2seq has the lowest WER. The broad two-dataset claim is therefore not supported by the paper's own LRS2 comparison table.

questions.q: What is the reported low-data benefit, and how is the 20% condition defined?
questions.answer: On CMLR, the reported CER decrease grows from 7.66 points with all training data to 9.63 points with 20%. The 20% condition is the first length-grouped subset: 27,262 sentences, each at most 11 characters.

questions.q: Which evaluation details limit reproducibility or interpretation of the headline results?
questions.answer: The paper omits run seeds/repetitions, speaker and session overlap, split sizes and exact date boundaries, teacher-ASR split exclusions, validation/checkpoint selection details, normalization, chance-level results, test-time LM use, and full protocols for cross-paper baselines.

questions.q: Does the reported lip-reading system require audio at use time?
questions.answer: The described task is muted-video sentence recognition; the audio speech recognizer supplies teacher representations and predictions for training-time distillation, while the student is the lip reader.

questions.q: Chung 2017 (WAS): where do 10.4% vs 39.5% CER come from, on which test set, and with the same training data?
questions.answer: Table 5 of Chung et al.: LAS audio-only 10.4% CER and WAS lips-only 39.5% CER on the LRS (BBC) test set, not LRS2; the audio-only model also trains on an auxiliary audio-only set.

questions.q: Petridis 2018 LRS2 visual-only CER/WER and LM use?
questions.answer: 42.1% CER, 63.5% WER; external LM (LibriSpeech + LRS2 pre-train text); LRW-pretrained front end.

questions.q: CSSMCM CMLR numbers and CMLR split?
questions.answer: CSSMCM 32.48% CER, WAS 38.93%; random 7:1:2 split, eleven hosts; no BLEU.

questions.q: Ren 2021: audio vs video teacher on LRS2; LIBS row; seeds?
questions.answer: No KD 57.5%, video teacher 53.4%, audio teacher 54.2%; final 49.2%; LIBS 65.3%; no seeds stated.

questions.q: Later best CMLR CER and LRS2 VSR WER?
questions.answer: Ma 2022: 9.1% CER CMLR-only, mean of ten runs; USR 2024: LRS2 VSR 16.0% (no LM), 15.4% (LM).
